items.body_md:
On August 7, four attorneys filed notices and motions to appear in Case No. 26-11169 before Judge Karen Owens in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware, with two pro hac vice admissions granted (Dkt. 71–72) and two motions pending (Dkt. 69–70), accompanied by a notice of appearance (Dkt. 68). The cluster of new entrants — five docket entries in a single day — signals that additional parties, beyond Industrial Accessories Company (which appeared July 31 via Dkt. 60) and Kuro Infrastructure Delaware, Inc. (whose counsel was admitted pro hac vice July 31, Dkt. 59), are now formally inserting themselves into the proceeding. The identities of those counsel are not disclosed on the face of the docket entries available; confirmation of who they represent will appear on the underlying appearance pleadings, which should be treated as the primary source once accessible.

That said, the directional read matters for recovery posture. 
As of the petition date, the debtor carried prepetition funded debt and guarantee obligations of approximately $70.8 million, comprising the approximately $50.9 million unsecured WVEDA loan guarantee (matured June 2026 and in default) and a purported $20 million unsecured Bilt note (in payment default), alongside a first-priority lien on substantially all of the debtor's assets granted to TRAG/RGE to secure more than $80 million of loans made to the debtor's non-debtor parent entities.
 With no unsecured creditors' committee yet appointed — confirmed by Dkt. 66 filed August 4 — the arrival of new appearing parties is the primary mechanism by which creditor constituencies are currently self-organizing. 
The debtor has stated it intends to investigate and prosecute estate claims against former management for the benefit of stakeholders,
 and the governance dispute between the Gassheimer/Quantum Pleasants faction and incumbent management — including 
Dynamic Finance Corp.'s delivery of a $75.64 million check purporting to fulfill all obligations under loan documents
 — remains unresolved on the docket. Creditors tracking recovery should monitor whether any newly appearing party has a nexus to either the TRAG/RGE lien position or the contested governance narrative, as that would materially affect whether the section 363 sale process runs cleanly or faces competing bids for control.

The procedural move for the week is straightforward: the docket is in its early-stage coalition-formation phase. 
Young Conaway Stargatt & Taylor LLP and Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer LLP are representing Omnis Pleasants LLC
 on the debtor side, and the next concrete milestone is the September 3 final hearing on the first-day critical operations orders covering employee wages, utility payments, and critical vendor payments — the session at which interim relief approved at the outset of the case will either be made permanent or modified.

items.body_md:
The 72-hour lookback window through August 8 is thin. Friday's five docket entries — Dkt. 68 through 72, plus an attorney-addition event — consist entirely of two pro hac vice motions (Dkt. 69, 70), their corresponding admission orders (Dkt. 71, 72), and a notice of appearance (Dkt. 68), all filed August 7. Yesterday's briefing flagged these filings and noted the identities of the admitting attorneys and their clients as unverified from the ground truth alone. That remains true today: no primary-source motion papers have been surfaced to confirm who entered the case. The pattern itself — a paired cluster of pro hac vice admissions arriving on a Friday, roughly three weeks into an active Chapter 11 — warrants continued attention, but absent confirmed identities it carries no actionable implication for the recovery posture.

No new press coverage dated August 8 has emerged. The most recent secondary reporting remains the August 5 Herald-Dispatch and Charleston Gazette-Mail articles already covered. Those pieces added regional texture to the governance fight — specifically, 
Gassheimer's account that TRAG/RGE filed counterclaims and a TRO motion in the West Virginia action on July 21 seeking to restore Nathan as Independent Manager, and that the West Virginia court denied that TRO on July 24
 — and they confirm that the Hindman management team has characterized 
the $75.6 million Dynamic Finance check as "uncertified," rejected for lack of transparency regarding the source of funds
. Neither development is new to the Delaware docket; they are factual anchors for the governance contest whose resolution, or escalation, will shape the August 19 objection period. One additional data point from regional coverage that has not been fully absorbed: 
prior management entered into a power purchase agreement in December 2025 with Element H, an affiliate owned by the Hodson family, at prices alleged to be below the cost of generation, with potential losses cited at $1 billion
 — __[News and Sentinel](https://www.newsandsentinel.com/news/business/2026/08/power-struggle-new-pleasants-power-leadership-fights-with-former-management-in-bankruptcy-filings/)__. That allegation is unverified (it appears in Hindman's declaration, not in a court ruling), but if substantiated it would materially widen the universe of potential estate claims and, by extension, the recovery pool available to unsecured creditors including the WVEDA.

Today's concrete task is a factual one: confirm from the underlying motion papers the identities of the counsel and parties behind Dkt. 69–72. Until those are known, the significance of Friday's appearance cluster — whether it represents a significant creditor, an adverse party organizing into the governance dispute, or a potential § 363 bidder — cannot be assessed. The next hard milestone is August 19, 2026, the objection deadline for the first-day operational orders set by Dkt. 57, followed by the September 3 final hearing before Judge Karen Owens in Courtroom 3, 824 Market Street, Wilmington, at 1:00 PM.

Today's docket movement is narrow but structurally legible: five entries filed August 7 — Dkt. 68 through Dkt. 72 — consist entirely of pro hac vice motions (Dkt. 69, 70) and their corresponding orders granting admission (Dkt. 71, 72), plus a notice of appearance (Dkt. 68) and an attorney-addition event. The filings do not identify the admitting attorneys or the parties they represent on the face of the ground truth provided, and those particulars are unverified; what is clear is that at least two new attorneys obtained leave to appear in the case today under D. Del. LR 9010-1. That pattern — a cluster of pro hac vice admissions arriving together — is typically a signal that a new constituency is organizing its representation, whether a significant creditor, a potential bidder, or a party with a stake in the governance dispute. Until the underlying motions are reviewed for the identity of counsel and client, the implications for the recovery posture remain uncertain, though the timing is notable: this activity arrives eleven days before the August 19 objection deadline for the first-day operational orders and twenty-seven days before the September 3 final hearing before Judge Karen Owens.

Dkt. 67, the Stretto affidavit of service filed August 5 and reported in yesterday's briefing, has since drawn regional press attention confirming the same headline figures already in the record. The Herald-Dispatch's August 5 report restates the governance contest between CEO Hindman's management team and the Gassheimer/Omnis Energy faction, and notes that 
the $50.9 million unsecured loan obligation to the West Virginia Economic Development Authority arises from a 2023 loan to Quantum Pleasants LLC to support the not-achieved conversion of the Pleasants Power Station into a hydrogen production facility.
 That framing matters to the WVEDA's recovery posture: the obligation sits unsecured, no committee has been formed to represent the general unsecured class (Dkt. 66), and the governance dispute — which turns on whether Gassheimer's appointment as interim director after 
Quantum Pleasants as sole equity owner removed Nathan as independent manager on July 20
 is valid — remains unresolved on the Delaware docket. The Herald-Dispatch coverage adds no new primary-source filings beyond what was covered yesterday, but its publication confirms the story is receiving sustained West Virginia press attention, which may accelerate pressure on the U.S. Trustee to convene a creditors' committee. __[Herald-Dispatch](https://www.herald-dispatch.com/news/omnis-pleasants-reports-600-creditors-70-in-wv-amid-uncertain-coal-plant-future/article_5b21adc9-1c75-433a-be51-5ed26f74a819.html)__

The next concrete milestone remains August 19, 2026 — the objection deadline for the first-day operational orders set by Dkt. 57 — followed by the September 3 final hearing at 824 Market Street, Courtroom 3, Wilmington, at 1:00 PM. The identities of the parties newly entering appearances today should be treated as a priority item to confirm from the underlying motion papers; if today's pro hac vice admissions represent a significant creditor or adverse party organizing into the governance dispute, the complexion of the August 19 objection period could shift materially.
